content:
Imagine Anna. She works in customer success at a B2B software company, and this week three customers have told her the same thing: they cannot find a quick way to schedule one post across several channels. She has an idea for how it could work. In most companies, that idea becomes a ticket. The ticket waits for a product manager, then a designer, then a slot in a sprint. By the time anyone shows a solution to Anna's customers, months have passed and they have learned to work around the problem.

AI makes it possible for Anna to build a working prototype herself, on the real product, in an afternoon. Yet most companies do not let her. Not because the tools are missing, but because of the objections that come up as soon as someone suggests it.

Why most companies never start

The objections are predictable, and each one sounds reasonable:

  • "Prototype code will end up in production."
  • "The design system will fall apart."
  • "People outside product and engineering are not technical enough."
  • "Public links will leak unreleased features."
  • "Customers will expect it next week."
  • "Everyone will build their own pet features."
  • "Who pays for it?"

Together they are often enough to keep prototyping with designers and engineers. Yet each of them can be solved in how you set things up. This is how we approached it at Swat.io, told through Anna's afternoon.

Anna sets up once

Anna opens the Claude desktop app and runs a single setup command. A Claude skill checks whether she has access to the playground on GitHub, installs what is missing and tells her what still needs attention. Ten minutes later she is ready, and she never has to open a terminal again.

The playground is a separate copy of our front end with mock data instead of a real back end. It cannot touch production data or live systems. That answers the first objection before anyone raises it: nothing Anna builds can end up in the product by accident.

Anna builds her idea

She types "Create a branch called multi-channel scheduling". Then she describes what she wants, much as she would explain it to a designer, and watches the preview update next to the conversation. Because the playground uses the real components and design system, the result looks and behaves like the product her customers already know.

She switches between three versions of the data with a parameter in the URL: a busy workspace, an empty one and the onboarding flow. That lets her check how the idea works for a long-time customer and for someone who has just signed up.

At one point she asks Claude to make a button stand out more. Claude uses an existing button style instead of changing the shared component. Instructions in the repository tell it to, and an automatic check would block any change to the design system anyway. Anything genuinely new goes to the design team, so the design system stays intact.

Anna shows it to customers

When she is happy with it, she types "Commit and PR". Claude replies with a public link. The link uses only mock data, is hard to guess and expires two months after the last change. Anna sends it to the three customers who raised the problem, introduced as an experiment and without a date attached.

The next day she has their reactions. Two like the direction; one points out a step that does not fit how their team works. That feedback goes into the project in Linear, where the product team decides whether and when to build it properly. Anna did not set the priority. She made sure the decision was based on something real.

The team improves the starting point

While building, Anna noticed that the mock data had no posts scheduled for the coming week. She fixes that on a separate baseline branch and opens a pull request. A front-end engineer reviews it, and from then on every prototype starts with better data. Engineers stay involved where it matters, in shared code, without having to review every prototype.

The cost of all this is a set of licences and some hosting for preview links. Compare that with one round of design and engineering time spent on an idea customers turn out not to want. The first avoided rebuild usually pays for the year.

How to set this up in your company

  1. Create a playground. Copy your front end into a separate repository with mock data and a few data states, and no access to production systems.
  2. Write instructions for Claude. Add a file that tells Claude how to run the preview, which components to use and what it must not change.
  3. Add a design-system check. Fail automatically when a prototype changes a shared component.
  4. Set up preview links. Give every pull request a public URL that expires after a period without changes.
  5. Write a setup skill. One command that checks access, installs what is missing and reports what is left.
  6. Arrange access. A GitHub account in your organisation and the Claude desktop app for everyone who should prototype.
  7. Write a one-page guide and record a short video. Show the handful of sentences people type, from branch to public link.
  8. Agree who reviews the baseline. Name a front-end engineer for changes to the shared starting point.
  9. Start small. Begin with three or four people from different teams, sit next to them, fix what confuses them, then open it up.

This is part 3 of the series The Bottleneck is moving. Part 4 covers how to get usability test results in 48 hours, and part 5 automated demo videos with Claude, Playwright and HeyGen. If you are setting up something similar in your company, I would like to hear how you approached it.
